Mies van der Rohe: Farnsworth House: only floor, roof, eight steel columns and glass; a wood core floats in the open plan.
Louis Sullivan: Guaranty/Wainwright type: base for shops, shaft for repeated offices, attic for machinery — each part's form expresses its function; terracotta ornament grows on the structure.
Le Corbusier: Villa Savoye — the Five Points: pilotis, free plan, ribbon window, free facade, roof garden.
Frank Lloyd Wright: Fallingwater — organic architecture: cantilevered trays anchored in a stone core, over the waterfall.
Walter Gropius: Bauhaus Dessau — art and technology: glass curtain workshop, bridge, school wing, studio tower.
Adolf Loos: Ornament is crime: bare white volumes; the Raumplan shows as interlocking cubes and roof terraces.
Robert Venturi: Vanna Venturi House — complexity and contradiction: a split gable, applied arch, and a decorated shed.
Antoni Gaudí: 'The straight line belongs to men, the curved line to God' — undulating facade, wavy iron balconies, parabolic arches, dragon-back roof, chimney warriors, mosaic spires and a trencadís bench.
Zaha Hadid: 'There are 360 degrees, why stick to one?' — one fluid, twisting skin flowing out into the landscape.
Frank Gehry: Deconstructivism — tilted, colliding volumes with scattered windows; a 'Ginger & Fred' pair, a crumpled metal sail and Gehry's fish.
Buckminster Fuller: 'Doing more with less': a geodesic dome (most volume, least material) and the mast-hung Dymaxion House.
Louis Kahn: Served & servant spaces, platonic geometry: brick cube with giant circular openings revealing an inner concrete wall, teak-panelled windows, servant towers and the Salk water channel.
Rem Koolhaas: 'Bigness': a continuous loop of program — two towers bridged by a base and an overhanging cantilever, wrapped in a structural diagrid that is densest where the forces are greatest.
Tadao Ando: Light, concrete and void: the Church of Light — a cross of light cut into fair-faced concrete (form-tie holes and panel joints), the slicing wall, and the cross on the water.
Aldo Rossi: Typology: the Teatro del Mondo floating on its barge, and the Gallaratese portico of thin piers.
Kisho Kurokawa: Metabolism: replaceable capsules plugged into service cores — a crane is delivering a new one.
Peter Eisenman: Autonomy of form (House VI): two shifted grids, a glass slot that splits the house, a column that hangs instead of supporting, and a red stair mirrored by an unusable upside-down green one.
Bjarke Ingels: 'Yes is more' — hedonistic sustainability: every flat gets a garden on the roof of the one below; the parking beneath wears a picture of Mount Everest.
Vitruvius: Firmitas, Utilitas, Venustas: a Doric temple — stylobate, columns with capitals, triglyph frieze, pediment with acroteria, and the altar in front.
Andrea Palladio: Villa Rotonda: perfect symmetry and harmonic proportion — four identical temple porticos, pedimented windows, statues and a ribbed dome.
Plato: Theory of Forms: the house is the ideal cube; the other perfect solids stand beside it.
René Descartes: Cogito ergo sum — the house laid out on the Cartesian x, y, z axes.
Immanuel Kant: Categorical imperative: one maxim willed as universal law — nine identical houses.
Jeremy Bentham: The Panopticon: cells in a ring, all visible from a central watch tower.
Martin Heidegger: Building Dwelling Thinking: the Todtnauberg hut, a deep roof sheltering the fourfold.
Ludwig Wittgenstein: Haus Wittgenstein: logical, austere, exactly proportioned blocks; tall precise windows.
Pythagoras: All is number: rooms are Fibonacci squares forming the golden rectangle; the tetractys in front.
Confucius: Harmony and order: a symmetrical courtyard house on a central axis (siheyuan).
Laozi: 'Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the emptiness at the centre that makes it useful.'
Albert Camus: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy': a house at the foot of the hill, the boulder near the top.
Gottfried Leibniz: 'Monads have no windows': windowless spheres in pre-established harmony.
J. W. von Goethe: Goethe's Gartenhaus (Weimar) and his 'Stone of Good Fortune' — sphere on cube. 'Architecture is frozen music.'
Socrates: 'The unexamined life is not worth living': the Stoa in the Agora, open to everyone.
Diogenes: Cynicism: virtue needs nothing — Diogenes lives in a barrel, lamp in hand.
Henry David Thoreau: 'Simplify, simplify': the 10 × 15 ft cabin at Walden Pond.
Heraclitus: Panta rhei — everything flows: a tower that keeps turning, on the river bank.
Friedrich Nietzsche: Übermensch: Zarathustra's mountain — the tower that keeps overcoming itself.
